query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray distance to achieve higher particle velocity during HVAF-i7 deposition will overcome the thickness limitation of FeCoNiCrAl bond coats.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a feedstock range of 15–45 μm as currently used in HVAF-i7 deposition.
generation.intervention: Set the spray distance to approximately 300–350 mm on the HVAF-i7 torch to increase particle kinetic energy.
generation.conditions: HVAF-i7 deposition on substrates (including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under conditions meant for high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy leads to improved particle melting and deposition efficiency, which in turn results in a thicker, well-adherent coating.
generation.mechanism: By shortening the spray distance, the particles experience less in-flight cooling and oxidation, resulting in higher impact velocity and better deposition. This improves the build-up of material, leading to a thicker coating while maintaining the desired oxidation resistance and adhesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline using 15–45 μm feedstock at the current settings, the adjusted spray distance will yield a significantly thicker coating with improved adhesion and minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.baseline: HVAF-i7 bond coats produced with 15–45 μm feedstock at the existing spray distance, which yield acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected under HVAF-i7 conditions with similar substrate geometries (down to 120 mm internal diameters) and service at elevated temperatures; deviations in powder properties or extreme geometrical constraints may affect performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement in deposition efficiency and resulting thickness gain are uncertain without empirical validation, and there may be trade-offs in oxidation behavior or coating microstructure that require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of HVAF-i7 deposition experiments using the 15–45 μm feedstock at various spray distances (for example, 200, 300, 350, and 400 mm) while keeping all other parameters constant. Evaluate the resulting coating thickness, adhesion, and oxidation level.
measurements: Oxide content and composition (via XRD/SEM analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If adjusting the spray distance to 300–350 mm does not yield a statistically significant (>20%) increase in coating thickness relative to the baseline, or if it results in unacceptable levels of in-flight oxidation or poor adhesion, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

Nb–silicide based alloy will require some kind of coating system. Alumina forming alloys that are chemically compatible with the Nb–silicide based alloy substrate could be components of such systems. The intermetallic alloys Nb1.7Si2.4Ti2.4Al3Hf0.5 and Nb1.3Si2.4Ti2.4Al3.5Hf0.4 were studied in the cast, heat treated and isothermally oxidised conditions at 800 and 1200 °C to find out if they are alumina scale formers. The alloys were designed using the alloy design methodology NICE and were required (i) not to have stable solid solution phase in their microstructures; (ii) not to pest and (iii) to form alumina scale. Their microstructures consisted of silicides and aluminides. Both alloys satisfied (i) and (ii) and formed thin scales at 800 °C. At 1200 °C the former alloy suffered from internal oxidation and formed alumina intermixed with Ti rich oxide beneath a thick “layered” scale of mixed oxides that contained Ti and/or Al and/or Si. There was no internal oxidation in the latter alloy that formed a thin continuous well adhering α-Al2O3 scale that was able to repair itself during oxidation at 1200 °C.
